institutionName: UiT The Arctic University of Norway

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: Location

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Wanting to experience life in the Arctic, especially midnight sun and polar night and all the snow and how people live with all that! And obviously also the mountains and fjords and nature overall :)

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, a lot of information is given beforehand and if you don't know something you can always ask or send an email, everyone is really willing to help

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Debut week gave information on important topics like registering in Norway, living with snow/darkness but also sports and other free time activities. But I think if you don't go to the orientation week it can be a bit difficult, although there are some emails sent out too. That week is also a great way to meet people so would definitely recommend arriving early enough

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: On campus housing isn't available but Tromsø isn't that big. As long as you're still on the island you're totally fine! Although I'd recommend trying to live close to the city centre and/or the university

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I got housing through Samskipnaden but was also quite lucky. Just apply as early as possible. But I also know that some people that applied before me didn't get anything so the system is a bit weird and it probably depends on your preferences as well. Might want to look for backup options on Facebook simultaneously. If you don't hear back from Samskipnaden, reach out as it might mean you didn't get a room

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You just look at the list of courses and then add that to your UiT application, really easy. There's a specific catalogue for courses that are open to exchange students. Although one of the courses I got approved was also not from the list so it's definitely possible to take other courses but probably depends per case

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The course catalogue and you could also just email any of the lecturers and the department or the mobility office, if you had some specific questions. They're happy to help

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful!

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The scheduling is pretty weird as every department/faculty has their own and they can overlap easily. Even though the semester started mid August, one of my courses didn't start until mid September so make sure to check the calendar. I was really busy in October for example because one of my courses was already ending so we had our project due and then two exams but the other course also had some deadlines at the same time.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Very similar to KU

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I think the quality of teaching is pretty good. Also a lot of group work and projects which was fun. A lot more readings though

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
SPL-3014 Arctic Cities Field Course
SVF-2107 Climate Change Adaptation

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Would recommend both! Arctic Cities especially is really cool because it's very applied and you learn a lot about Tromsø as a city and meet a lot of planners from the municipality. But you also get some really cool knowledge on cities in the Arctic overall and the region of Northern Norway. As the name suggests lots of field trips.
Climate Change Adaptation was interesting too, also pretty applied and very focused on the Arctic and Norway. If you don't have any or only little knowledge about climate change I'd definitely recommend it, otherwise a lot of it will be repetition as it is an introductory course to climate change and only Bachelor's level

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There's a student sports organization that offers pretty much any sport imaginable and there's also a gym on campus. Every other Friday there's free waffles. A good number of clubs like board game clubs, knitting, etc. Also a lot of conferences that are usually open to students too. ESN does a lot of events as well

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Tromsø is a very active and dynamic city, there's so many events and things happening that you can go to! Pubquizzes (highly recommend the one at Storgata Camping every Tuesday), karaoke nights, comedy nights, cinemas, small festivals and concerts, swimming pool, saunas. Also check Facebook for more specific events like flea markets or some shows

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Hiking!! As much as possible before the snow comes, the nature is just ABSOLUTELY breathtaking. Would also recommend sailing and camping (no need to bring tent or sleeping bag as you can rent that for free at Turbo). When the snow is there, I'd definitely say cross country skiing, it's pretty easy to pick up and SO easily accessible as there are tracks all over the island and on Kvaløya (again equipment can be rented at Turbo or bought for very cheap at Rebell, a big second hand store). Also lots of nice trips from Tromsø like Sommarøy, anything on Kvaløya, some glacial lakes and glaciers (Lyngen Alps), Senja, and of course cabins all over. For some trips you need to rent a car but it's pretty easy and the journey is already kind of the destination, as you're just driving with breathtaking and never-ending views of mountains and fjords

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It's not that different compared to Denmark so very easy, the biggest difference was just that people are a lot more outdoorsy

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Sports and other social clubs

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The focus on nature and being outdoors

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Go outside as much as you can, the seasons change so quickly and the semester will be over before you know it...
Remember to start taking your vitamins early so you don't get depressed when the sun doesn't rise anymore.
Consider applying for two semesters right away if you can because you might want to stay longer once you get there and realize how amazing it is! :)
Bonus: if you have the time, take the train instead of the plane, the views on the way there are amazing!! Also pretty easy to go from Copenhagen, you just transfer in Stockholm and then take the night train to Narvik and from there a bus to Tromsø. But might want to plan an extra day as backup as the nighttrain isn't that reliable and delays are common

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just reach out to people if something isn't working out and you will probably have a solution to your problem very quickly

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Honestly the nature with all its outdoor activities and living in the Arctic. Also seeing the northern lights everywhere, even from my room, was pretty cool!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Leaving :(

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I honestly didn't find the darkness that bad. You just kind of adjust to a new rhythm/routine as it gets dark so early that it's totally normal to still do things in the afternoon, like skiing or studying, otherwise your day would only be a couple hours long. Even during polar night it's not pitch black outside 24/7 but it does get lighter for a few hours every day. I was luckily done with my courses pretty early so I had more time to focus on friends and social activities and didn't have to study for exams in the darkness, then it would've been a very different story probably... The snow also reflects a lot of the darkness, so it always seems lighter than it actually is, especially on cloudy days, and on cloudless days you usually have northern lights! :)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
